title: The foundation chain — counting, reading, and common mistakes
subtitle: The starting chain is where most beginners gain or lose stitches before the first row
excerpt: The foundation chain is the series of loops cast on before the first row. Getting the count right, reading which loop to insert into on the first row, and avoiding twisting the chain are the three things that most often go wrong at this stage. This tutorial covers all three.

glossaryTerms.definition: The starting row of chain stitches made before the first working row. The foundation chain sets the width and is not counted as a row. The first row works into it, typically starting from the 2nd or 3rd chain from the hook depending on stitch height.

content.text: problems are the most common source of a crooked or wrong-width first row. The three issues to address before starting the first row are: the chain is the right length, you know which loop to insert into, and the chain is not twisted.

Do not count the slip knot. Do not count the loop currently on the hook. Count each V-shaped loop along the front of the chain — each V is one chain. The loop on the hook is always the working loop and is never counted as part of the chain.
Reading the chain — which loop to insert into
The front of the chain shows a row of V-loops. The standard insertion for the first row is under the top strand of each V only — the loop closest to you.

The back of the chain has a single bump (back bar) behind each V. Inserting under this back bar instead of the V leaves the V-loop visible as a neat edge on the foundation — used when a tidy bottom edge matters.
Insert under both top strands of the V (under both loops of the V) for the most secure foundation — this is less common but the most stable.

items.symptom: Foundation chain is twisted when work begins
items.cause: Chain allowed to spiral before the first row begins
items.fix: Lay the chain flat on a surface before starting row 1. All V-loops should face the same direction. Start the row before picking the chain up.

items.symptom: First row is shorter than the chain count suggested
items.cause: Accidentally skipping chains near the start, or starting from the wrong position
items.fix: Count the chain after making it, before starting. For a dc row, the first dc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook. For a tr row, the first tr goes into the 4th chain from the hook.

content.text: Foundation dc (also called chainless foundation dc) skips the chain entirely and works the foundation row and first row simultaneously. It produces a more elastic edge than a chain foundation and is the preferred start for garments that need stretch.
